chunks: And from him, also, from Fadala ibn Ayyub, from Muawiya ibn Ammar, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who has a debt: is it upon him to perform Hajj? He said, 'Yes, indeed the Hajj of Islam is obligatory upon whoever is able to walk among the Muslims.
And indeed, most of those who performed Hajj with the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) did so on foot.

And the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) passed by Kura' al-Ghaim, so they complained to him about fatigue and hardship, and he said, 'Tighten your girdles and ride (or mount), so they did that, and it went away from them.'"

Because the meaning of these two reports is the encouragement to perform Hajj on foot and the attraction to it, and that it is preferable when one has the capacity, even though the word 'obligatory' was used in the last report, because we have clarified in other places in this book that what is preferable to do may be called 'obligatory' even if the obligatory meaning that incurs punishment for leaving it is not intended. And many reports have been narrated regarding the encouragement to perform Hajj on foot, including what he narrated:

key_terms.حَجَّةَ الْإِسْلَامِ: The Hajj of Islam (the obligatory pilgrimage)

ai.seo_question: Is Hajj obligatory for someone who has debt, and is walking preferred over riding?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi clarifies that while Hajj is obligatory for those with the means, walking is the preferred mode of travel, as evidenced by the Prophet’s companions who mostly walked during his era. The text distinguishes between strict legal obligation (wajib) and recommended preference (awla), noting that the Prophet permitted riding to alleviate hardship, thereby balancing spiritual devotion with physical capacity. This reflects the Shia juristic principle that what is 'most fitting' is often linguistically termed obligatory to encourage its performance.
